Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

cdrgam 0.4.0

  • New simulate_effect() draws coefficient vectors from the approximate posterior and evaluates the same functionals as estimate_effect() for each draw. Use it for uncertainty in nonlinear summaries of an effect, such as the lag at which a response peaks.

cdrgam 0.3.0

  • Sparse Gaussian REML diagnostics report newton_step_max, the largest coordinate of the Newton step on the log smoothing-parameter scale, and predicted_decrease_floor, the smallest criterion change the practical convergence test treats as resolvable. In a reading-time model the largest gradient component was 0.033 against a tolerance of 1e-4, while the predicted decrease was 1.2e-5 against a floor of 3.6e-3.

  • Boundary reduction treats a smoothing parameter that the outer Hessian classifies as an upper or lower boundary like one at the optimizer’s box limit: only a score favoring less smoothing, at an upper boundary, blocks reduction. Such a parameter is flat along its own direction, so the optimizer can stop short of the limit with a score that still points past it. In a reading-time model, one penalty of a by-subject interaction IRF stopped at log smoothing parameter 24.04 with a score of -3.3e-4, three times the gradient tolerance; the fit ended without converging, and autosimplification removed the whole term instead of the one inactive subspace.

  • Chunked cross products assemble each chunk’s design over its nonempty columns only, slicing rows from transposed components through their column pointers, and place the chunk’s product back at the global indices. A chunk touches a few groups, so work proportional to every column grew with columns times chunks. On 988 subjects of a reading-time model (111,238 coefficients, 354 chunks), accumulation fell from 939 to 524 s, with row extraction and assembly falling from 701 to 229 s and an identical cross product.

  • Sparse Gaussian fits log their full named smoothing-parameter vector at the end of each optimizer restart and at the final solution, and while the criterion improves at most every 15 minutes, so that an interrupted run leaves a recent best in its log. The reporter previously showed only the first six values.

  • Sparse Gaussian setup builds the stored system pattern with one merge of the cross product instead of one per penalty, and extracts each chunk’s design rows from a transposed copy of every ungrouped sparse component, so a chunk no longer scans the whole column-compressed matrix. On 200 subjects of a reading-time model with 52 penalties, system assembly fell from 145 to 42 s and cross-product accumulation from 106 to 97 s, with an identical pattern and identical coefficients.

  • Automatic sparse gradient selection now measures before choosing finite differences. When its estimate favors them, a fit times one warm objective evaluation and one exact gradient at the starting point and decides from those times. The estimate scaled the first evaluation, which includes one-time setup, by a Schur cost ratio that assumes an evaluation costs about one core factorization. On 200 subjects of a reading-time model with 200 subject blocks around a 580-coefficient core, it predicted 620 s per exact gradient against a measured 5 to 10 s, so finite differences were chosen at about 50 to 100 s per gradient.

  • Chunked cross products no longer store the exact zeros of their dense blocks. When a chunk held rows of several subjects, the dense block stored a zero for every pair of coefficients from different subjects; on 20 subjects of a reading-time model that added 389,312 stored zeros. These zeros coupled the subject blocks in the stored system pattern and caused every Schur factorization to fail.

  • The sparse Schur factorization accepts explicit zeros between coefficient blocks in the stored system pattern, and its block layout is validated against that stored pattern. Previously every Schur factorization of a model whose pattern held such zeros failed, and each evaluation silently fell back to a full Cholesky factorization with a fresh symbolic analysis. On a 111,238-coefficient model this made every evaluation far more expensive in memory than the Schur path. A fallback from Schur to a full factorization is now reported in the fit log.

  • Sparse Gaussian fits handle smoothing parameters at which the penalized system is not numerically positive definite, as happens when penalties on terms with nearly overlapping column spaces approach zero. Such a system no longer triggers a fresh full Cholesky factorization, which failed in the same way and allocated a second factor. The factorization is instead retried with a relative diagonal ridge of 1e-12, 1e-10, or 1e-8; the log reports each stabilized evaluation, and a fit whose final solution needed a ridge warns that terms are likely confounded there. L-BFGS-B now always receives cdrgam’s finite-difference gradient, including with one worker, and that gradient is not evaluated at a point whose objective has just failed. On a 111,238-coefficient model, the first L-BFGS-B step reached the smoothing-parameter bounds; one evaluation there failed, and about 100 more failed while the gradient was computed around it before the job exceeded its memory.

  • When a sparse Gaussian factorization fails, the fit log now reports the solver’s message and the log smoothing parameters of the failing evaluation, so the point can be reproduced outside the fit.

  • Memory-limited parallel plans now charge each forked worker the parent process’s full resident memory in addition to its own allocations, because R’s garbage collector marks every live object and so causes a child to copy nearly all inherited pages. A sparse fit also measures how far resident memory rises during its first objective evaluation and charges each gradient worker at least that much. For a 111,238-coefficient model, the earlier estimate of about 40 GB per worker allowed two finite-difference workers, and the job exceeded a 256 GB allocation. The sparse fit log reports the selected gradient workers and the memory charged to each.

  • Chunked cross products now multiply columns that are nonzero in most rows of a chunk, such as population IRF terms, as a dense block with BLAS, and only the remaining active columns with the sparse product. For a 200-subject version of a 126,058-coefficient reading model, one 10,000-row chunk took 0.48 s instead of 9.7 s, with results equal to within 4e-15 relative. This is the dominant cost of forming the penalized system for such models.

  • The dense location-scale inner fit now counts a stalled line search as converged when even its smallest step could not change the objective by more than its numerical floor. Its absolute gradient tolerance could lie below that floor after predictor rescaling, so small rescaled fits ended with “Dense gaulss LAML optimization ended at an invalid fit”.

  • Sparse backends now add chunked cross products pairwise when forming the penalized system and the PIRLS and location-scale information matrices. Adding each chunk to a running total rewrote the whole accumulated matrix once per chunk; for a 155,698-coefficient model with 205 million system nonzeros and 355 chunks, cross-product accumulation took about 2.7 hours. On a smaller model with the same structure, pairwise accumulation was 7.4 times faster.

  • A sparse location-scale fit keeps its optimizer endpoint unless an earlier evaluation is lower by more than 1e-9 times the criterion. Previously any lower evaluation, including one that differed only by inner-solve noise, replaced an endpoint that had met the gradient tolerance and marked the fit as nonconverged.

  • rescale_predictors now defaults to TRUE in prepare_cdrgam() and cdrgam(), so continuous predictors and lag coordinates are divided by their training standard deviations unless rescale_predictors = FALSE. Effect estimates and plots are still reported in native units. center_predictors already defaulted to TRUE.

  • The exact phase of sparse location-scale fits now solves inner fits to sparse_control$exact_inner_relative_tolerance (default the tighter of 1e-11 and inner_relative_tolerance). At the previous 1e-8 relative tolerance, inner-fit error of about 0.002 on a criterion near 10^6 exceeded the remaining trust-region improvements, so fits stalled and were reported as nonconverged.

  • The safeguarded trust-region optimizer used by the sparse backends starts assessing convergence as soon as three successive rejected steps, each no longer than 1e-5 times the largest absolute parameter (at least 1e-5), lose more criterion than the model predicted. When the caller supplies a curvature assessment, it certifies the result as it did after the radius collapsed; otherwise the optimizer reports “converged to criterion precision”. It previously kept shrinking the radius until it reported “trust radius became too small”.

  • Sparse Gaussian location-scale REML fits warm up with extended Fellner-Schall smoothing-parameter updates (Wood and Fasiolo, 2017) instead of stochastic scores whenever the hybrid gradient is selected. Each update needs one inner fit and penalty traces but no outer score or line search, and smoothing parameters still moving toward a limit start the exact phase on the search bound, where the projected trust region treats them as inactive. sparse_control$warmup chooses "efs", "stochastic", or "none", and efs_maxit limits the updates.

  • Generalized sparse REML fits now compute an outer Hessian by central differences of their exact score after optimization (sparse_control$hessian = "gradient", the default; "none" skips it). It enables the boundary classification and profile bounds, the optimizer_stopped_short and indefinite_outer_hessian diagnostics, and unconditional inference for generalized fits, which previously had no outer Hessian. The cost is two score evaluations per outer parameter.

  • The exact generalized GCV gradient now streams batches of inverse columns through the same routine as the Gaussian analytic Hessian. It previously stored a dense selected inverse over the union of penalty supports, whose memory grew with the square of that union.

  • fit_diagnostics() distinguishes an optimizer that stopped short from a genuinely indefinite outer Hessian. Negative curvature along a single smoothing parameter, or a Newton step that would still lower the -2 REML criterion by more than 0.1, is reported as optimizer_stopped_short, with the parameters in hessian_negative_directions and the estimate in predicted_decrease; the fit warning suggests final_newton = TRUE. Negative curvature that mixes several smoothing parameters is still reported as indefinite_outer_hessian.

  • Sparse Gaussian REML fits accept sparse_control$final_newton = TRUE, which refines the smoothing-parameter optimum with safeguarded Newton steps using the exact gradient and analytic outer Hessian after the outer optimizer stops. It holds boundary smoothing parameters fixed, descends along negative curvature, and stops at a positive-definite optimum or after newton_max_steps. It is on by default; it is skipped, and recorded as skipped_memory, when the analytic Hessian does not fit the automatic memory budget. Set final_newton = FALSE to keep the outer optimizer’s result.

  • The penalty log pseudo-determinant and its derivatives now use a stable reparameterization (Wood 2011) within each penalty block. Penalties are grouped by scaled size, each group’s range is fixed from its unit-normalized sum, and smaller penalties are carried into the remaining null space. The previous single eigendecomposition dropped the eigenvalues of a penalty more than about 10^14 times smaller than another in the same block, which changed the computed rank and made the criterion discontinuous.

  • Unconditional sparse inference (unconditional = TRUE in vcov(), estimate_effect(), and test_effect()) now stops with an error when the outer Hessian is not positive definite after boundary smoothing parameters are excluded. It previously inverted an indefinite block whenever the inversion succeeded numerically, which could add negative or unbounded smoothing-parameter variance to the covariance without warning.

  • The sparse condition indicator now measures collinearity rather than scale. It is min_i L_ii^2 / A_ii over the Cholesky pivots of the penalized system A, which is one minus the largest squared multiple correlation of a coefficient with those eliminated before it. It previously squared the ratio of the smallest to the largest pivot, so a single very large smoothing parameter could trigger ill_conditioned_penalized_system with no collinearity present. Gaussian REML fits also leave out the coefficients of penalties classified as on the boundary, because a very large rank-deficient penalty makes its own coefficients nearly dependent; fit$sparse$condition_indicator_full keeps the value over all coefficients. For one 3.5-million-observation fit the reported indicator moved from 1.8e-16 to 3.9e-4.

  • Saved sparse fits no longer contain a copy of the prepared design. The stored expanded mgcv formula took its environment from the function that built it, which held the design, so saveRDS() wrote the full design with every fit. For a 3.5-million-observation fit this was 6.1 of 6.6 GB. The formula now uses the environment of the design’s ordinary formula.

  • Sparse Gaussian REML fits now separate smoothing parameters on the boundary of their range from genuine outer-Hessian problems. A parameter is on the boundary when its absolute log value is at least sparse_control$boundary_hessian_log_sp (default 8) and its whole outer-Hessian row is at most boundary_curvature_tolerance (default 0.05). Such parameters are listed in fit$sparse$convergence$hessian_boundary, excluded from the positive-definiteness check and from unconditional covariance, and reported as a boundary_variance_components note in fit_diagnostics() that does not change outcome. Previously they made the Hessian indefinite and produced a warning. Flat directions that mix several smoothing parameters are still reported as an indefinite Hessian. hessian_min_eigenvalue now refers to the interior block; hessian_full_min_eigenvalue keeps the full-matrix value.

  • For each smoothing parameter at its upper boundary, a variance component estimated as zero, the fit records a profile bound: the smallest log smoothing parameter whose -2 REML criterion stays within qchisq(2 * boundary_profile_level - 1, 1) of the optimum, with the other smoothing parameters fixed. With sparse_control$boundary_sensitivity = TRUE, the fit at the bounds is stored, and estimate_effect() and test_effect() accept boundary = "bound" to check whether conclusions depend on treating those components as zero.

  • The sparse backend’s analytic outer Hessian and exact GCV gradient use much less memory. They previously kept A^{-1} S_j for every smoothing parameter at once, which took memory proportional to the number of penalized coefficients times the summed penalty supports. They now solve for one batch of inverse columns at a time, accumulate every trace that uses the batch, and discard it. Batches follow the block structure of the penalties, so grouped penalties are split by group, and penalties that share a support share one solve. Peak memory scales with the number of penalized coefficients times the batch width, which is usually trace_chunk_size or the size of the largest penalty block. cdrgam.max_analytic_hessian_elements now counts the elements of one batch. The hessian = "auto" memory estimate counts every array the batched computation allocates, and the analytic Hessian is selected when that estimate is at most 75% of available memory and leaves at least 1 GiB free. The previous rule allowed at most half of available memory.

  • estimate_effect(composition = "total") now sums the full hierarchy of ungrouped terms below the selected term: terms on the same by covariate whose predictors are a subset of its predictors, with the same linear or smooth treatment. Previously only a single-predictor smooth term or a time-varying term found a parent, so irf(x, z, k_p = list(NULL, 3)) was returned without irf(x), irf(z), or irf(1). The total effect of a linear single-predictor term now includes irf(1), as it already did for a smooth one. Under grouping = "conditional", the grouped deviations of the hierarchy terms are added at the same level.

  • estimate_effect() gains reference, which subtracts the functional at reference axis values and carries the joint covariance into the standard errors. A reference value of a linear predictor gives the effect of changing that predictor at each value of its moderators; a reference value of a moderator gives differences between interaction curves. A predictor set to NA or "default" is left at the model default, so the terms that involve it drop out of the reference.

  • The deviation composition is removed. It returned the same values as term; grouped deviations remain available through grouping.

  • New test_effect() computes joint Wald tests that an estimate_effect() functional is zero over its grid, using a rank-truncated pseudo-inverse.

  • The sparse backend now reports exactly collinear IRF terms as rank deficient regardless of rounding. Its identifiability check previously passed whenever CHOLMOD returned a factor, including after warning that the system was not positive definite or when rounding left a near-zero positive pivot, so some rank-deficient models were fitted without error. A CHOLMOD warning now counts as a failed factorization, and a pivot that is a negligible fraction of its diagonal entry, below rank_tol, is reported as rank deficiency. The ratio does not depend on predictor scaling.

  • Linear IRF predictors, including binary ones, are now centered by default at their means over the training history links. irf(1) is then the response to an event with average linear predictors, linear terms are deviations from it, and removing irf(1) removes the average-event response. Previously irf(1) was the response at zero on the coded scale, which for a strictly positive predictor is an extrapolation, and the two terms were strongly collinear. New fits of existing formulas therefore estimate a different irf(1) and different lower-order interaction terms; total predicted responses are essentially unchanged, except in models that omit irf(1) or lower-order interaction terms, whose meaning changes. Use center_predictors = FALSE to restore uncentered predictors, or irf(center = ) per term. Fits made before this change keep their uncentered meaning. effect_catalog() reports the stored centers.

  • Solver checkpoints resume when the stored floating-point summaries of the model differ from the current ones only by rounding error, as happens when a fit resumes on a node with a different CPU or BLAS configuration. Structural fields must still match exactly, and the mismatch error now names the fields that differ.

  • The sparse backend builds ti() terms with one random-effect factor margin, such as ti(time, subject, bs=c("cr", "re")), as sparse per-level blocks. These terms were previously expanded to a dense design, which could exhaust memory with many factor levels. The design and penalties equal those of mgcv::ti() up to column order. Other ti() forms still use the dense ordinary design.

cdrgam 0.2.0

  • Establishes the first public development release of the current CDR-GAM implementation.
  • Provides native, dense block, and sparse fitting backends for continuous-time deconvolutional generalized additive models.
  • Supports Gaussian, generalized, and Gaussian location-scale models with stream-aware prediction, inference, diagnostics, and effect estimation.
  • Adds bounded-memory history construction, checkpointed optimization, and resource-aware parallel execution.
